APPEALS CONSOLIDATED;
PETITIONS FOR A STAY GRANTED IN PART;
NOTICE OF HEARING
Western Watersheds Project, Idaho Bird Hunters, and the Idaho Wildlife Federation
(collectively referred to as WWP) have appealed from and petitioned for a stay of five Final
Decisions, each dated April 22, 2005 and issued by the Field Manager, Owyhee Field Office,
Bureau of Land Management (BLM). The Idaho Native Plant Society (INPS) has separately
appealed and petitioned for a stay of the same five Decisions. The Decisions provide for renewal
of five 10-year grazing permits to the permittees of the Hardtrigger Allotment (Allotment). The
Decisions are all based on environmental assessment #ID130-2005-EA-759 (EA) and are nearly
identical, except for the name and address of the permittee and the amount of grazing use
authorized for each of the permittees (hereinafter the Decisions are collectively referred to as the
“Decision”). The Decision decreases authorized active grazing use to 1,560 animal unit months
(AUM’s), which is a 16% reduction. It also provides for the construction of at least 15 range
improvements, including spring developments, pipelines, troughs, fences, and cattle guards.
Upon completion of a particular fence and two pipelines, a grazing rotation system will be
implemented so that spring grazing is periodically deferred in the spring pastures. Pending
completion of those three improvements, pasture rotation will occur in accordance with an
“Interim Management” system.
In each of its appeals, WWP raises the same issues. Likewise, INPS reiterates the same
arguments in each of its appeals. Given these facts, as well as the fact that the permittees graze
the Allotment in common, the appropriate course of action is to consolidate the five appeals of
WWP and the five appeals of INPS. Accordingly, THE APPEALS ARE HEREBY
CONSOLIDATED.
On June 6, 2004, BLM filed a response in opposition to each of the petitions for a stay.
For WWP and INPS (hereinafter “Appellants”) to prevail on their petitions, they must show, in
accordance with 43 C.F.R. § 4.471(c)(2), sufficient justification based on the relative harm to the
parties if the stay is granted or denied, the likelihood of Appellants’ success on the merits, the
likelihood of immediate and irreparable harm if the stay is not granted, and whether the public
interest favors the granting of the stay. The party seeking the stay bears the burden of
4

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
demonstrating that a stay is warranted under each of the regulatory criteria. See 43 C.F.R.
§ 4.471(d); Oregon Natural Resources Council, 148 IBLA 186, 188 (1993).
To achieve success on the merits, Appellants must meet their burden to demonstrate, by a
preponderance of the evidence, that the Decision is unreasonable or does not substantially
comply with the provisions of the Federal grazing regulations found at 43 C.F.R. part 4100. See
43 C.F.R. § 4.480(b); Eason v. BLM, 127 IBLA 259, 262 (1993). A BLM decision may be
regarded as arbitrary, capricious, or inequitable only where it is not supported by any rational
basis. Wayne D. Klump v. BLM, 124 IBLA 176, 182 (1992).
In balancing the likelihood of movant's success against the potential consequences
of a stay on the other parties it has been held that "it will ordinarily be enough that
the plaintiff has raised questions going to the merits so serious, substantial,
difficult and doubtful, as to make them a fair ground for litigation and thus for
more deliberative investigation." Hamilton Watch Co.v. Benrus Watch Co., 206
F. 2d 738, 740 (2d Cir. 1953), quoted in Placid OilCo. v. United States
Department of the Interior, 491 F. Supp. 895, 905 (N. D. Texas 1980).
Wyoming Outdoor Council Inc., 153 IBLA 379, 388 (2000) (quoting Sierra Club, 108 IBLA,
384-85 (1989)).
Based upon a preliminary review of the record and pleadings, and as more fully explained
below, the petition for a stay is granted in part and denied in part. To the extent that the Decision
authorizes range improvements, including but not limited to fences, pipelines, springs, wells, and
troughs, the stay is granted. With regard to the remainder of the Decision, the petition for stay is
denied.
Grazing System
Appellants have not shown that the balance of harm warrants issuance of a stay regarding
the grazing system identified in the Decision. Appellants argue that the Decision increases
stocking rates and authorizes either 2,197 or 1,879 AUM’s (WWP’s Appeal, at 4, 26).
Appellants confusion over the AUM’s authorized through the Decision is understandable. At
first glance, Table 15 of the EA appears to list the season of use for most of the permittees as
being seven months in length from April 1 to October 31. Based on that season of use, BLM
would be authorizing 2,197 AUM’s. However, a careful examination of the Decision reveals
that the regularly scheduled season of use is five months long from April 1 to August 31,
resulting in 1,560 authorized AUM’s. Grazing until October 31 will occur only if grazing in
certain pastures is deferred from the regularly scheduled season of use to August 7 through
October 31 to allow perennial bunchgrass an opportunity to improve in condition (EA at 14, 22).
5

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
Appellant’s conclusion that table 14 of the EA authorizes 1,879 active AUM’s is
probably based on erroneously multiplying the total number of cattle by the 28-day period from
April 1 to April 28 twice (624 AUM’s) rather than once (312 AUM’s). This error is
understandable because the same 28-day period is identified in Table 14 in two separate
locations, once for the Hemingway Butte pasture and once for the Alfalfa pasture. However, the
undersigned reads table 14 to indicate that cattle will simultaneously graze both pastures during
the same period of time consuming only 312 AUM’s.
The Decision’s authorization of 1,560 AUM’s represents an approximately 16-percent
reduction in active AUM’s from the amount authorized prior to issuance of the Decision under a
1999 BLM decision. The 1999 decision would govern grazing on the Allotment pursuant to 43
C.F.R. § 4160.3(d), if a stay were entered.
Appellants are aware of this circumstance and argue that grazing under the 1999 decision
would be preferable for a number of reasons. However, Appellants’ arguments in this regard are
largely based on their reservations about the range improvement projects authorized in the
Decision.
As explained below, the range improvement projects authorized in the Decision are being
stayed. As a result, the “Interim Management” system will apply because implementation of the
ultimate grazing system detailed in the Decision is dependent upon completion of some of the
range improvements (Decision at 8-9).
The major difference between the “Interim Management” system and the previous
grazing management system is the reduction in AUMs. That reduction is likely to be beneficial
to the resources at issue. Consequently, granting a stay of the Decision’s components other than
the range improvement projects is likely to be more harmful than denying such a stay both in
general terms and with regard to the Appellants’ interests in minimizing any degradation of the
land and resources which their members enjoy. It follows that the Decision, except for those
provisions authorizing the range improvement projects, should not be stayed because Appellants
have not shown that the balance of harms favors granting a stay.
Range Improvement Projects
Page eight of the Decision authorizes at least 15 range improvement projects, including
spring developments, pipelines, troughs, fences, and cattle guards. WWP argues that the EA is
deficient because it does not adequately describe the location, scope, and impact of each of these
projects.
The most extensive description of these projects is found at pages 16 and 17 of the EA.
There, the projects are described in one word sentences, e.g.: “Develop water at the old mercury
mine site into a short pipeline to an aluminum water trough at T.1N, R.4W, Section 29.”
6

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
Accompanying maps help identify the general location of these projects but add nothing more to
their descriptions.
The question is whether BLM’s description and analysis of the range development
projects is sufficiently thorough to meet the “rule of reason” standard. In Wade Patrick Stout, et
al., 153 IBLA 13, 21 (2000), the Interior Board of Land Appeals described the rule of reason
standard as follows: “In determining whether an EA promotes informed decision making, a ‘rule
of reason’ will be employed. The query is whether the EA contains a ‘reasonably thorough
discussion of the significant aspects of the probable environmental consequences’ of the
proposed action and the alternatives thereto.” Id. (internal citations omitted).
The problem with BLM’s cursory and vague treatment and descriptions of these projects
is that BLM has not given the reader a reasonably objective understanding of what the projects
will entail. For example, telling the reader that “a short pipeline” will be developed does not add
much to the readers understanding of the pipeline or its length.
While the EA offers multiple assurances that construction of the range developments will
have little or no long-term impacts, there is a paucity of facts and analysis of impacts to support
those assurances. Instead, BLM offers promises of mitigation of any impacts such as the
following:
It is essential that mitigation be applied to ensure that trough placement would not
occur where the potential exists for livestock and/or wild horses to create new trail
routes through existing plant sites or increase use within these plant sites. This
mitigation would also include a thorough pre-project (during the design and layout
phase) inventory in order to approve trough(s) placement. Sensitive plants are
presently unknown from other proposed project areas; however, all of these areas
will be surveyed for potential locations in the spring during peak flowering,
during the design and layout phase for each project. Project development would
be modified to ensure that no or minimal impacts would occur.
(EA at 26).
These types of mitigation measures are properly part of the planning process and should
be implemented in conjunction with locating and constructing the projects. However, mitigation
measures are not the same thing as a reasonably thorough description of the projects and their
potential impacts, which is what the rule of reason requires. See Wade Patrick Stout, 153 IBLA
at 21.
BLM’s deciding official, the interested public, or a reviewing tribunal (Reviewers) should
have a better understanding of the range development projects than the EA communicates.
In this case BLM is essentially telling the interested public that the planned range projects are
7

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
insignificant and will be constructed correctly. BLM’s veracity in this regard is not being
questioned by this forum. However, informed public involvement is one of the primary goals of
the NEPA process. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 122 IBLA 334, 341-42 (1992). NEPA
does not envision requiring the interested public to trust government assurances that everything
will be alright.
The EA does not explain how springs and wells will be developed. It does not explain
how long pipelines will run from springs to troughs, whether those lines will be buried, and, if
so, how deeply. The Decision authorizes reconstruction of the Windy Point pipeline spur-lines
into Hemmingway Butte, but does not explain where those spurs will be located or how long they
will run. BLM does not need to explain these projects in exhaustive detail but should at least
give Reviewers a basic idea of what the projects involve.
Another more ominous possibility arising from these ambiguities is that BLM may not
fully realize the scope or impacts of the projects it is authorizing. This concern is magnified by
BLM’s statement that the conditions of springs in the Allotment are not well documented (EA at
27). This is particularly relevant here because the Decision authorizes the development of at
least four springs (Decision at 8). Appellants note that after the spring developments authorized
in the EA are complete, only two of twenty springs identified on public lands in the Allotment
will remain undeveloped (WWP Appeal at 3). The EA does not describe how much water these
springs produce, whether they support riparian systems or whether adequate water will remain
available for those systems after the springs are developed. The EA indicates that spring
development will have a positive effect on conditions in the Allotment but this conclusion must
be considered in view of BLM’s own acknowledgment that spring conditions are largely
unknown.
Appellants’ allegations raise serious questions regarding BLM’s compliance with the rule
of reason requirement that an EA be supported by a reasonably thorough discussion of the
significant aspects of the probable environmental consequences of the proposed action and the
alternatives thereto. The EA does not define the authorized range developments in a reasonably
tangible fashion. Without this information, it is difficult to conclude that BLM has taken a good-
faith, objective, hard look at the environmental consequences of the proposed developments and
considered all reasonable alternatives. Consequently, Appellants have shown a sufficient
likelihood of success on the merits with respect to the proposed range development projects.
Appellants have also shown that the relative harm to the parties and likelihood of
irreparable harm favor granting a partial stay covering those proposed projects.
[W]hen a decision to which NEPA obligations attach is made
without the informed environmental consideration that NEPA
requires, the harm that NEPA intends to prevent has been suffered.
* * *
8

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
It is appropriate for [a tribunal] to recognize this type of
injury in a NEPA case, for it reflects the very theory upon which
NEPA is based – a theory aimed at presenting governmental
decision-makers with relevant environmental data before they
commit themselves to a course of action. This is not to say that a
likely NEPA violation automatically calls for an injunction [or
stay]; the balance of harms may point the other way.
* * * [T]he harm [caused by a NEPA violation] consists of the added risk
to the environment that takes place when governmental decisionmakers make up
their minds without having before them an [adequate] analysis (with prior public
comment) of the likely effects of their decision upon the environment. * * * [A
tribunal] should take account of the potentially irreparable nature of this
decisionmaking risk to the environment when considering a request for
preliminary injunction or [stay].
Sierra Club v. Marsh, 872 F.2d 479, 500-01 (1st Cir. 1989) (quoting Commonwealth of
Massachusetts v. Watt, 716 F.2d 946, 952 (1st Cir. 1983)); see also Injunctions Under NEPA
After Weinberger v. Romero-Barcelo And Amoco Production Co. v. Village of Gambell, 5 Wis.
Envtl. L. J. 1 (1998). Thus, BLM’s likely NEPA violation entails a potentially irreparable risk to
the environment that must be considered in assessing the likelihood of irreparable harm and the
relative harm to the parties.
That risk constitutes a substantial harm associated with denying the stay petition with
respect to the proposed development projects. If at least a partial stay is not granted, Appellants
argue that its members will be harmed by the loss of their ability to experience the lands in
question without ongoing degradation of important public resources. Appellants’ concerns
resonate against the backdrop of the poorly described range development projects. Because the
EA does not adequately define the range development projects, NEPA could be violated two-
fold. First, by the authorization of projects which have not been fairly submitted to NEPA
procedures, and second by potential actual impacts which were not foreseen or considered in the
EA.
Additionally, the harm which may result from allowing construction of the poorly
described range improvement projects outweighs the temporary harm that may be incurred by
temporarily allowing grazing without the range improvement projects during the comparatively
short time it will take to resolve Appellants’ appeal.
Finally, the public interest favors granting a partial stay. Before BLM makes an
irretrievable commitment of public resources, the issue of whether BLM complied with NEPA
should be fairly litigated and deliberately investigated to insure that the purposes of NEPA are
served. Given that BLM failed to thoroughly discuss the significant aspects of the range
9

ID-130-2005-026 through 035
development projects and their environmental consequences, it is my determination that the
Decision is not well-informed with respect to the proposed developments.
Based upon the foregoing, THE PETITIONS FOR A STAY ARE HEREBY PARTIALLY
GRANTED WITH RESPECT TO THOSE PORTIONS OF THE DECISION WHICH
AUTHORIZE RANGE IMPROVEMENT PROJECTS AND THE PETITIONS ARE
HEREBY DENIED WITH RESPECT TO THE REMAINING PORTIONS OF THE
DECISION.
Notice Of Hearing
The hearing in this matter will commence at 1:00 p.m. on Monday, September 19,
2005, in or near Boise, Idaho and will proceed thereafter to its conclusion. I am sending today a
letter to BLM’s Owyhee Field Office, pursuant to the provisions of 43 C.F.R. § 4.473, requesting
personnel there to arrange for appropriate hearing facilities and to issue and serve an appropriate
hearing notice which will specify the precise place of hearing.
James H. Heffernan
Administrative Law Judge
